newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union ratifies GM labor deal, ends strike.
newsitem.headline: Canada union ratifies GM labor deal, ends strike.

text.p: About 26,000 General Motors Corp unionized workers in Canada ended a 20-day strike by ratifying a tentative labor agreement between the world's largest automaker and the Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) union.

CAW president Buzz Hargrove told a news conference the GM Canada membership voted 88.7 percent in favor of a deal which provides for the sale of two parts plants, but saved about 1,800 jobs from being outsourced.

Hargrove said 14,621 workers voted on the contract, of which 10,097 production workers and 2,876 skilled trades workers voted in favor of the contract. One thousand six hundred and forty-eight production and skilled workers voted against the contract.
"This appears to be the highest turnout we've had in the history of our ratification votes," the union leader said.

The union will open serious negotiations with the last of the big three North American automakers, Ford Motor Co's. Canadian subsiduary, for a 1996 labor agreement and will announce a strike deadline on Monday.
Approval of the new pact was expected to clear the way for GM to reach a quick labor agreement in the United States with the much-larger United Auto Workers (UAW) union.

Some UAW sources said on Wednesday a deal could be reached in a matter of days. The U.S. talks, which affect 215,000 hourly workers, were moving quickly when the Canadian strike started on Oct. 2 and stole the spotlight from UAW President Stephen Yokich.

"I think without question they would have settled by now, but the UAW did not want to undermine the Canadian union's negotiating stance," said Harley Shaiken, a professor of labor relations at the University of California-Berkeley. "The (UAW) negotiations will move very quickly."

Sources close to the talks said they thought GM would agree to guarantee jobs for 95 percent of its UAW work force -- nominally the same terms that rivals Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp. agreed to -- but that level may exclude some U.S. parts plants now up for sale.
As in Canada, the major unresolved issues in the United States include GM's ability to shift work to outside suppliers, known as outsourcing, and the sale of parts plants.

In the Canadian settlement, GM won the right to sell parts plants in Windsor and Oshawa, Ontario, employing 3,850. The automaker also wants to sell a door hardware plant in Flint, Mich., and an interior trim plant in Livonia, Mich., that together employ 2,100 UAW members.
UAW officials said the buyer for all four of the U.S. and Canadian plants was Joseph, Littlejohn and Levy, a New York-based investment firm that owns other auto parts firms.
GM also has said it was studying options for other parts plants. It has about a dozen facilities it considers "troubled."
The three-year Canadian pact, in addition to allowing GM to sell the Ontario parts plants, includes a pledge by the automaker to recognize limits on outsourcing.
The union, in turn, made a major concession by accepting that GM's business plan may require deviance from a pattern agreement reached in September with Chrysler.
Some of GM's Canadian workers will return to their jobs on Thursday and all of the automaker's Canadian operations will be running normally by Nov. 4, union officials said on Wednesday.

"So we could begin as early as tonight bringing some of our component people in Oshawa into work," said GM Canada spokesman, Greg Gibson. "Then tomorrow we would start bringing some of our assembly people in and then we'll stage it over the next day or so."
The walkout by Canadian workers idled 20,000 GM workers in the United States and Mexico and paralyzed suppliers across North America.
